doc.title: Marty Sheller interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 9, 2022

chapter: Growing up and discovering Latin music
title: Teenage listening in Newark and the Cafe Bohemia double bill
summary: Starting with West Coast jazz, a delayed 'bing' reaction to a Miles Davis record from Buddy Terry, and seeing Max Roach and Art Blakey at the Cafe Bohemia.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I want to take you back a little bit. You grew up in Newark, is that correct?
Yes. Newark, New Jersey. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
Do you recall, let’s say you’re 12, 13, 14. What music made a lasting impression with you?

It began with the West Coast players, a group of friends that I had that we used to get together and play, we were listening to the guys out of the West Coast: Shorty Rogers and Stan Kenton, those kind of people. And I’ve thought about that and I realize that the reason probably was it was easier to understand. And matter of fact, when I went to high school one of the fellas in my high school was a very good tenor saxophone player and he laid a Miles Davis record on me and it was “Blue ’N’ Boogie,” one of those extended 45s part 1 and part 2. The musician’s name was Buddy Terry, and he gave it to me. I took it home and I listened to it and, Monk, it went right over my head. I just didn’t understand what was going on because I had been listening, like I said, to the West Coast players. So I just put it in with the rest of my music and it sat there for about a year, a year and a half. And when I got into high school I just happened to cull through my record collection again and I listened to it. And bing! It hit me. I like sort of said how could I have fallen asleep on this record? And that led me to try and investigate some of the players that were on it, and I was lucky enough to have gone to a famous old jazz club called The Café Bohemia with a double bill, catch this double bill — there was the Art Blakey Quintet and the Max Roach Quintet. Now my friend and I walked in at the last number of Max Roach’s Quintet which was a beautiful “Valse Hot.” That was with Sonny Rollins and Kenny Dorham. And that knocked me out, the idea that they could swing so hard in 3/4. When they got off the stand Art Blakey came on and that was being some of the hardest bop ever, that was with Jackie McLean on alto and Bill Hardman on trumpet, and I was so impressed — oh and plus the stage at the Café Bohemia was very high, like maybe five feet high, and at the end of the set, which was the end of the night, Blakey sat on the edge of the stage with his legs dangling over and he gave his famous “Support Jazz” speech. And I was so impressed. So when I walked outside I looked up at the marquee and I said I’m not familiar with these guys. I wrote down the names and that started my collection of the East Coast players.
Terrific story. I remember that Café Bohemia is mentioned in Cannonball Adderley’s entrance into the jazz world also.
